archetype.name: Game Manager (scheme-constrained)
archetype.definition: A second-year passer whose offense keeps the ball short and on the ground. He is asked to protect the ball and move the chains rather than push it downfield, and so far he isn't getting enough out of those short throws to justify the caution.

report.headline: Cleaner process, same empty production: the Titans are hiding Ward, not unleashing him
report.take:
Cam Ward's second season looks like a coaching staff trying to shrink the job for its young quarterback. Tennessee passes 9.4 points less often than situation predicts, 30th in the league. Ward's intended air yards sit at 6.93, and his aggressiveness has dropped to 9.13% from 12.6% as a rookie. The results haven't followed. His -0.129 EPA per dropback ranks 37th of 45, his 5.67 yards per attempt ranks 40th, and his 1.9% touchdown rate ranks 42nd. The 1-6 record belongs to an offense ranked 31st in EPA, not to him alone. He still hasn't shown he can lift it.

The shape of his throws explains most of it. The safe stuff is losing. His 37 passes behind the line of scrimmage have cost -13.7 EPA at -0.371 a play, so the screen game is a drain rather than an outlet. His 21 deep attempts have been worse: a 14.3% completion rate, a CPOE of -24, two interceptions and -15.7 EPA. In between sits the one part of his game that works. On 43 throws of 10-19 air yards he is at +0.301 EPA per play, +12.9 in total. That is the throw a franchise quarterback lives on, and he makes it. The under-center package is a separate problem: 32 plays at -0.49 EPA, with four of his five interceptions.

The raw lines hide real growth in how he plays the position. His bad-throw rate is down to 13.5% from 17.6%. His pressure-to-sack rate has fallen to 20.8% from 32.2%, and his 5% sack rate ranks 12th. His CPOE is up 1.9 points on last year. He is getting rid of the ball faster, behind a line that allows the fourth-lowest hit rate in football. That is a quarterback learning the pocket. Two things undercut it: the gains aren't turning into yards or touchdowns, and his interception rate is up even as his aggressiveness fell. The last three weeks also bent the wrong way: a CPOE of -7, a 3.4% interception rate and 4.02 adjusted net yards per dropback. That stretch includes an 11-of-22 day at Indianapolis. He then played his best game of the season, +5.9 EPA, against a Cleveland defense ranked 7th, so a slump verdict would be premature.

Where it heads depends on whether Robert Saleh's staff lets him throw the intermediate ball more and the screens less. Carnell Tate has become the clear go-to target at +0.197 EPA per target on 51 looks. With Calvin Ridley and Tyjae Spears both out, the target tree narrows even further onto Tate. Expect volume to rise as the Titans keep trailing. His efficiency when down nine or more (-0.111 EPA) has been better than in one-score games (-0.211). That makes him a passer whose box scores may improve more than his play does.

strengths.title: The intermediate window works
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards produce +0.301 EPA per play, a success rate near 49% and a CPOE of +1.9. This is timing and anticipation over the middle levels of the field, the hardest throw to teach. It is also the strongest argument that the scheme is undercutting him by not calling it more. On 43 attempts it is a real signal rather than a fluke, and it should hold.

strengths.title: Sharper pocket management than as a rookie
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate has dropped from 32.2% to 20.8%, and his bad-throw rate fell by 4.1 points. He is processing faster and taking fewer drive-killing sacks. Good protection helps, but it doesn't explain a drop this large. Year-two improvements in pocket habits tend to stick.

strengths.title: A real connection with Tate
strengths.body: Carnell Tate leads the team with 51 targets and turns them into +0.197 EPA each, a clear outlier in a passing game where most options are negative. Elic Ayomanor (+0.167 on 21) is the other productive read. With Ridley out, Tate's role only grows.

concerns.title: No deep ball whatsoever
concerns.body: A 14.3% completion rate and -24 CPOE on 20+ air-yard throws is not just conservative play-calling. When he does take the shot, he misses badly or throws it to the other team. His rookie season was also low-efficiency, so this isn't a new hole. Until it changes, defenses can squat on everything short of the sticks, which his -2.48 air yards to the sticks invites.

concerns.title: Interceptions up, under center especially
concerns.body: His interception rate is 2.4%, up from his rookie year even though he is throwing less aggressively. Four of the five came on just 32 under-center plays, which carry -0.49 EPA. The play-action and under-center package is clearly not working for him. The fix may be as simple as calling less of it, but it is a costly blind spot right now.

concerns.title: Screens and checkdowns are a net negative
concerns.body: The 37 throws behind the line have bled -13.7 EPA at a 21.6% success rate. That is the price of a scheme that manufactures easy completions without creating yards after the catch. This one is more on design and personnel than on Ward, and losing Spears, a -0.181 EPA-per-target outlet, removes part of it.

trend.note: Game-level EPA has swung from -16.9 against Houston to +5.9 against Cleveland within three weeks. The last three games carry a CPOE 5.9 points below his season mark, even though the most recent game was his best.

nextGame.headline: Ten-point road underdogs facing a pass rush that finishes
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati's defense ranks 5th against the pass by EPA and 2nd in sack rate. It is also 4th against deep passes, which shuts off the throw Ward already can't hit. The opening is underneath: the Bengals rank 30th in EPA allowed on short passes and give quarterbacks 279.7 yards a game, 28th. Their offense is 6th in EPA and the league's most pass-heavy, so the Titans should be chasing points. That brings volume, and Ward has been steadier when trailing big than in close games. Against this rush, the cleaner pocket habits he has built get a real test, but the matchup favors the Bengals.

Tennessee is down two of Ward's regular pieces. Calvin Ridley, a 54%-snap receiver, and Tyjae Spears, his top back in the passing game, are both listed out. That funnels even more of the passing game to Tate, Wan'Dale Robinson, Ayomanor and Gunnar Helm. On the other side, Kyle Dugger is out, but he played only a part-time safety role, so it barely changes the coverage.

keyMatchups.title: Bengals pass rush vs. Ward's pocket
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati gets home on 8.9% of dropbacks, second-best in the league. Ward has cut his pressure-to-sack rate sharply this year, and a game where Tennessee has to throw a lot is the real test of that. If drives die on sacks, the empty-volume scenario gets worse.

keyMatchups.title: Short-area softness vs. his short game
keyMatchups.body: The Bengals allow 0.219 EPA on short throws, 30th in the league. Ward's quick-game efficiency has been poor, mostly because of the behind-the-line throws. Quick throws to Tate and Robinson past the line, rather than screens, are the path to a respectable afternoon.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end opportunity for Helm
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati has let lead tight ends score 3.9 PPR points a game over their averages, 30th in the league. It also sees a higher-than-normal share of targets go to the position. Helm hasn't been efficient (-0.054 per target), but with Ridley and Spears out, the matchup points his way.

nextGame.watch: How often he throws in the 10-19 yard window rather than behind the line. That ratio is the clearest read on whether the staff is starting to trust him.

restOfSeason.body:
The sustainable part is the pocket work: fewer sacks and fewer wild misses, built over a full rookie season and seven more starts. What won't move much without a scheme change is the ceiling. An offense this run-leaning and this short-throw-heavy caps his yardage and touchdown output, and he hasn't shown a deep ball that would break it. His 1.9% touchdown rate is low enough that some upward drift is likely, especially with more trailing game scripts. His interception rate could also ease as the under-center turnovers prove partly a small-sample cluster. Expect roughly 165-215 passing yards a game with a touchdown about every other game, and little rushing value.

The bigger question for his development is whether the intermediate success gets more of the call sheet. If it does, his efficiency could climb toward league-average territory by December. If not, he stays a high-floor-for-mistakes, low-ceiling passer piling up volume while behind. The returns of Ridley and Spears matter mostly for depth of options. Tate is already the passing game.
swingFactors: Whether the staff opens up the intermediate passing game
Calvin Ridley's return and Tate's continued growth
How often negative game scripts force volume

confidence.note: Seven starts plus a full rookie season paint a consistent picture, but the depth splits and late-game numbers rest on small samples.
